  • Industry observers note that armed officers from ICMBio, Brazil’s environmental protection agency, moved down corridors lined with bird pens.
  • It has been revealed that the dawn raid this past May 27 marked the collapse of what not long ago was hailed as an audacious conservation experiment: a multimillion-dollar attempt to resurrect a vanished species in its native habitat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The raiding party set out in darkness.

Leaving behind the industrial city of Petrolina in northeast Brazil, the eight-vehicle convoy, escorted by two Federal Police SUVs, crossed the São Francisco River and, for two hours, traversed the Caatinga, a stark landscape of thorn scrub, cactuses and drought-stricken ranch land. At dawn, the procession turned off the highway and jolted down a dirt road to a fenced compound. The police presented a judicial order. Then the vehicles drove up to a cluster of buildings housing 103 birds that rank among the rarest animals on Earth: Spix’s macaws, luminous blue parrots that vanished from the wild a quarter-century ago.

Industry observers note that armed officers from ICMBio, Brazil’s environmental protection agency, moved down corridors lined with bird pens. A cacophony of screeches and beating wings erupted as the team went from cage to cage, trapping the macaws in nets. Some birds bore feathers that had bleached white; others were marked by pink patches where necrotic plumage had rotted out. One bird’s beak was grotesquely deformed, its upper mandible split into keratinous shards. All were manifestations of beak and feather disease, which is caused by an avian circovirus that can ravage the immune system, attack fast-growing tissues and lead to an agonizing death. The task force members scanned a microchip beneath each bird’s skin that indicated which had tested positive for the virus and which negative. As aviary employees watched in silence, the officers placed the healthy birds into transport cages, carried them out to their convoy and rode off in a cloud of dust.

It has been revealed that the dawn raid this past May 27 marked the collapse of what not long ago was hailed as an audacious conservation experiment: a multimillion-dollar attempt to resurrect a vanished species in its native habitat. Bred back from a tiny captive population, the blue parrots, made famous by the 2011 animated hit Rio, had begun a tentative recovery. In 2022, 20 birds were released to great fanfare into northeast Brazil’s Caatinga wilderness, where many adapted, expanded their territory and—most remarkably—began to breed, flashes of blue cutting through the muted landscape. Four hundred more macaws were scheduled for release over the next 20 years, and breeding and planning for those releases continued until 2025. For a time, the project seemed to support the once unthinkable idea that extinction, often the consequence of habitat loss and human predation, might be reversible.

But the Brazilian government now says that the organizers, a German nonprofit called the Association for the Conservation of Threatened Parrots (ACTP), botched the program and tried to deceive the authorities about the extent of its problems. Dozens of captive-bred macaws awaiting release have been quarantined. The project has been put on hold, its future in doubt. A criminal investigation has begun into ACTP’s activities in Brazil. Some conservationists point to the collapse as a textbook case of good intentions gone awry. What had been a carefully choreographed attempt to return animals to the wild has become an urgent effort to understand what went wrong.

The fallout was tangible in Petrolina. At the veterinary campus of the Federal University of the São Francisco Valley, ICMBio staffers, accompanied by the police, unloaded the carriers and placed the birds in a temporary holding facility. Reports about the raid had already exploded across social media. One parrot enthusiast in the United States claimed that Brazil was preparing to “euthanize” the 34 infected macaws left behind, but officials I talked to insisted the rumor was untrue.

At the entrance to the veterinary school, where the healthy birds were kept, I donned a hazmat suit and received a spray-on dose of disinfectant. Then I followed Pietro Martins, a 24-year-old ICMBio birdkeeper, into the aviary. Up close, the macaws were smaller than I expected, with lustrous blue feathers, ruffled gray head plumage and a preternatural alertness. They fluttered around their cramped cages, vocalizing noisily, hanging upside-down by their talons, clinging to the wire grid with their curved beaks. Martins slipped bowls of pumpkin seeds and bright-colored food pellets inside each cage and stepped back into the corridor. The birds would be monitored and tested for a year, Martins told me, to make certain that they hadn’t contracted the lethal pathogen. In the meantime, Brazilian scientists would closely observe the area surrounding the reintroduction site for evidence of an avian pandemic. The region is home to thousands of parrots, Fábio Muniz, the chief of Brazil’s environmental crime unit, told me. “Any number of species could become infected.”.

Bird collectors began capturing and trading the Spix’s macaw—named for the 19th-century Bavarian biologist who first brought a specimen to Europe—in the early 1900s. Though Brazil banned wildlife exports in 1967, and the international Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora tightly restricted the endangered species trade eight years later, a black market linked bird trappers to syndicates smuggling macaws across four continents. “As in all collecting fraternities, there is an obsessive element,” Tony Juniper, a British ornithologist and chair of the conservation group Natural England, told me. “‘Have I got the rarest, have I got the best?’ With the Spix’s macaw, this has been an glitch for a long time.” By the 1980s, as hydroelectric dams and agricultural encroachment swallowed up much of the bird’s native range, the few remaining Spix’s macaws appeared to concentrate in a woodland area 60 miles northeast of Petrolina, around the town of Curaçá.

One morning in late May, I set out to visit the wilderness where the Spix’s macaw had made its last stand. Driving out of Petrolina, I reached Curaçá, a sunbaked riverside cattle town, and pushed deeper into the Caatinga. Candelabra-like mandacaru cactuses and patches of xique-xique, a thick-bodied succulent bristling with needle-sharp spines, covered the flat landscape. I turned down a dirt track to meet Adonai Martins, Pietro Martins’ grandfather, an octogenarian rancher who had watched the species dwindle into oblivion. A slender man with a weathered face and a white beard, Adonai greeted me on the porch of his home in a clearing in the bush. He wore a chapéu de couro, the leather cowboy hat of the Brazilian vaqueiro. He had spent his entire life in the Caatinga. As a boy, he said, “I looked up and saw flocks of eight or ten blue macaws flying overhead. They were prettier than the maracanas”—green macaws with blue-tinged wings and tail feathers—“and for the traffickers, they were worth a lot more money.

Recent findings suggest that spix’s macaws nest in caraibeiras, yellow-flowering trees with deep roots that grow along the Caatinga’s seasonal riverbeds. In the 1980s, a trapper nicknamed Carlinhos das Araras—Carlos of the Macaws—hired local men to string nets over known caraibeira hollows. “He rode around in his car and watched where the macaws went,” Adonai Martins recalled. “After that, it was no problem to take them.” By 1990, only a single male Spix’s macaw remained. “I was so used to seeing them fly over my house, from riverbed to riverbed,” Adonai said. “And suddenly, they were gone.”.

But conservationists dreamed of resurrecting them. Over the next two decades, geneticists and field experts rolled out a global dragnet to find every Spix’s macaw trafficked out of Brazil and every captive-bred specimen held in private collections. In one case, they tracked down “Presley”—a male in his 30s—at the home of an elderly rare-bird collector in Denver. Presley succumbed to old age before he could be integrated into a breeding cohort, but Brazilian veterinarians extracted his testicles (nestled inside the avian body), which were frozen so scientists could try to harvest viable genetic material in the future.

Industry observers note that the momentum shifted in 2016, when Brazilian officials began a partnership with ACTP. Under its founder, Martin Guth, ACTP had accumulated by far the world’s largest collection of Spix’s macaws. Guth, a former pet-shop employee and debt collector with financial backing from such partners as Belgium’s Pairi Daiza zoo and Jurong Bird Park in Singapore, had an unconventional past, and his organization was alleged by the Guardian and some conservationists to have trafficked in parrots. But, Cláudia Sacramento, an ICMBio scientist, told me, “The government knew the only way it could come back with a reintroduction program was to deal with ACTP.” Brazil purchased private land and carved out two reserves totaling nearly 300,000 acres near Curaçá. Guth contributed $1.4 million to build a reintroduction center and another $180,000 a year to support the operation. He also brought in international experts led by Cromwell Purchase, a noted South African aviculturist then working on a Spix’s macaw breeding project in Qatar. Purchase, who relocated to Brazil, became the project’s scientific director.

In 2020, ACTP flew 52 Spix’s macaws to Brazil. Purchase had set up large training cages where captive-bred birds would learn the skills necessary to survive in the wild. ICMBio helped provide 15 captured maracanas, otherwise known as blue-winged or Illiger’s macaws, a smaller and fairly common species in central and eastern Brazil, to serve as “mentors.” This kind of mixed-species interplay had never been attempted in a parrot reintroduction program, but in the 1990s the last wild Spix’s macaw had paired with a wild female blue-winged counterpart, suggesting that the two species could interact well. (The fertilized eggs laid by the blue-winged macaw didn’t hatch.) And other avian projects had fostered teacher-student relationships, for instance raising captive-bred California condors with wild-caught adults to teach them how to spot and feed on carrion, soar long distances, and develop other skills and behaviors they would need upon release.

In a recent development, for 15 months, the Spix’s pupils lived within sight of their mentor birds but in a separate enclosure to prevent interspecies pairing. Then, for the final four months of pre-release training, the birds were placed together inside a kind of avian boot camp: a 23-foot-high, 155-foot-long “flight and release module” filled with natural perches and fruit-and-seed-producing vegetation. There, under the guidance of the mentor birds, the Spix’s macaws shifted their diets from food pellets to seasonal nuts and fruits, flew alongside the wild birds, and learned to sound alarms and duck for cover when owls, hawks, falcons and other predators hovered hungrily over the mesh-protected cage. Trainers selected the 20 fittest Spix’s, each between the age of 3 and 7, for the first release.

Recent findings suggest that pietro Martins, then working at the reintroduction center in his role with ICMBio, remembers the jubilation that swept through the valley on June 11, 2022. A video captured by ACTP preserved the moment. The first macaw to be set free, fitted with a radio transmitter, hesitated on the threshold. Then it unfurled its blue wings and climbed steeply into the sky. Seven more Spix’s, all radio-tagged, and eight blue-winged macaws followed that day; a second group, including 12 Spix’s and seven blue-winged macaws, were set free six months later.

According to recent reports, to make sure the birds wouldn’t starve, Purchase and his team suspended two feeders stocked with local fruits, flowers and seeds outside the release cage and set up more on the branches of nearby trees. As birds paired off and began exploring the gallery forests, ACTP staffers tracked them around the clock from two 19-foot-tall towers and from ground points throughout the area. The mixed flock formed a cohesive unit outside the cages, but the blue-winged macaws’ mentoring couldn’t save all the Spix’s. Nine of the 20 vanished or died during the first three years, some picked off by predators, others electrocuted by uninsulated power lines. But the 58 percent first-year survival rate eclipsed that of other avian rewilding projects, according to Thomas White, a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service official who served as a technical adviser to ACTP. Even more promising, the wild- released Spix’s macaws began to breed, hatching chicks in their ancestral homeland for the first time in a generation. A single prolific male, logged as “Male No. 7,” fathered six chicks across two separate pairings in 2023 and 2024. To help the breeding, ACTP teams installed 12 nest boxes in caraibeiras and wrapped slippery zinc bands around the trunks to thwart attacks by opossums, marmosets and small wild cats. At the time, White lauded the initiative as “the most carefully planned and executed psittacine reintroduction that I have ever seen.”.

One afternoon, Pietro Martins and I trekked into the heart of the now disused Spix’s macaw reserve: a dry creek bed that transforms briefly into a torrent during the rainstorms that lash the Caatinga between November and March. Fifty-foot caraibeiras flanked the sand-filled watercourse, their trunks pocked with nesting hollows hammered out by crimson-crested woodpeckers. Martins pointed to ropes dangling from high branches, which he and other ACTP researchers had used to shinny up the trees and check on eggs and chicks.

Recent findings suggest that when Martins joined the project, he had no idea about Brazil’s complicated history of avian conservation. Because Brazil stopped issuing export permits for its native birds after 1967, the government regarded all captive specimens abroad since then as contraband. But in the 1990s, the Brazilian government offered amnesty to private owners and breeders of Spix’s macaws around the world, promising not to go after them in court in exchange for their cooperation with future captive-breeding recovery programs. (Many clandestine owners came forward.) Purchase, like other ACTP staffers, shrugged off any lingering taint of past illegality. Working with Guth, he told the environmental news site Mongabay in 2024, represented the “best option, and in fact the only option” for successfully returning the species to the wild.

Guth’s trajectory is a study in self-reinvention. As a boy in East Berlin in the 1970s and ’80s, he cleaned a neighbor’s bird cages and, as a 10-year-old, filled his family’s barn with budgies and parakeets. He was drawn to the birds’ exotic coloring and, as he told me recently, their affordability. “In those days, you could buy a budgie for 5 deutsche marks,” or about $2.50, he noted as we sat at a Berlin café on a brisk September morning. “A macaw would cost you 5,000,” or about $2,500. A solidly built man with a bald head, a ruddy complexion and a trimmed salt-and-pepper beard, Guth agreed to meet me only after persistent encouragement from colleagues; he felt he’d been burned by the press, and he was guarded and initially on edge. He scowled when I asked about his youth, saying in accented, near-fluent English that he’d recounted it “many times before.”.

Guth fled to Hungary before the Berlin Wall fell and eventually settled in Hamburg to work as a birdkeeper in a pet shop. But by the mid-1990s, he transitioned into organized crime, collecting debts and, in at least one instance, extorting a nightclub owner for protection money. Once, according to court testimony, Guth briefly held two men hostage to strong-arm them into paying what they owed. In September 1996, a German court handed him a five-year prison sentence for extortion-related offenses. “I was a youngster,” Guth later told the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung.

Upon his release, Guth was vacationing in the Canary Islands when he saw his first Spix’s macaw at Loro Parque, a zoo with a well-known parrot collection. He soon redirected his energies into his childhood obsession: to acquire and breed rare parrots, framing his enterprise as a means of saving the birds from extinction. In 2005, he purchased three Spix’s for €15,000 from a Geneva aviculturist who could no longer care for them. The next year, he established ACTP, constructed a state-of-the-art aviary in the village of Tasdorf outside Berlin, and negotiated deals with private collectors and international wildlife regulators.

Sources indicate that he soon began wooing Al Wabra Wildlife Preservation in Qatar. Its owner, Sheikh Saud bin Mohammed Al Thani, a billionaire collector of art, meteorites and rare animals, had started with a few dozen Spix’s macaws and by expert breeding grew the total number of birds to 120. After the sheikh died in 2014, Guth persuaded the royal’s children to bequeath him the birds, giving him control of 90 percent of Spix’s in the world. Over the next several years, Guth bred dozens of parent-raised chicks and created a deep reserve for rewilding. The facility grew to house hundreds of specimens. It earned Guth a moniker: “The Parrot King.”.

In a recent development, did you know? Prelude to an extinction.

In 1995, with a single Spix’s macaw surviving in the wild, conservationists released a captive-bred female into Brazil’s Caatinga wilderness in hopes the pair would mate.

The birds soon paired off, but before long the female disappeared; years later, a local resident noted he spotted the small blue corpse beneath a power line, though its fate was never confirmed.

Sources indicate that the male, the world's last wild Spix's macaw, disappeared in 2000. The Spix’s macaw was declared extinct in the wild in 2019.

Sources indicate that yet his success remained shrouded in mystery. “He is uncredentialed as a wildlife conservationist, zoologist or scientist, and he emerged with financial backing to acquire the most endangered parrots in the world,” says Paul Reillo, founding director of the Rare Species Conservatory Foundation in Florida. Guth’s ascent attracted scrutiny among conservationists and news organizations alike. A 2018 exposé in the Guardian claimed that Guth, under the banner of conservation, was quietly acquiring rare black cockatoos—valued at tens of thousands of dollars apiece—from the Australian government and funneling them to wealthy collectors. A 2020 Audubon investigation detailed how ACTP had extracted rare, state-protected red-necked Amazon and imperial parrots from the Caribbean island of Dominica after Hurricane Maria in 2017 against the objections of local conservationists. Concluding that ACTP provided Guth with a sheen of legitimacy for a lucrative, transnational enterprise, the article’s author, Brendan Borrell, acknowledged that Guth’s affection for parrots seemed genuine. “Guth may have pure intentions when it comes to protecting parrots,” he wrote, adding that he detected “some morsel of sincerity beneath his bluster, a belief that conservation can pay for itself—and that the ends, when it comes to his beloved birds, justify the means.”.

Recent findings suggest that when I met him, Guth denied illegally trading in rare species, and he folded his arms defensively when I asked him about such charges. “You are presenting me with the same s--t from all the other articles,” he stated. Instead, he wanted to talk about the Spix’s macaw. By the time he began collecting them, he told me, the global population had dwindled to just 52 captive-bred specimens. “I was told that the bird is coming to an end. I had to do something.”.

Lorenzo Crosta, a veterinarian who works with ACTP, told me that Guth’s commitment to the birds speaks for itself. “Martin is genuinely passionate about this species, and his dedication has led to remarkable success.” Vladislav Marcuk, the manager of ACTP’s Tasdorf aviary, states, “Without Martin, I think we wouldn’t even have a conversation about reintroduction.”.

In 2022, Guth, overcome with emotion, stood outside the release center in Brazil and watched his birds soar into the wilderness. “It’s so amazing,” he enthused on the video capturing the occasion, his voice cracking. “Waiting for 16 years for this moment. ... Now we have blue skies in the Caatinga again.”.

Recent findings suggest that by the end of 2023, however, Pietro Martins sensed trouble. A upcoming government took power in Brazil, and ACTP officials felt that it had turned against the reintroduction program. Long bureaucratic delays and a worldwide outbreak of avian flu stalled shipments of Spix’s macaws from Germany and scotched planned release dates; ICMBio also claims that many birds received in Brazil were too old or infirm for wilderness survival. This shattered the timeline of ACTP’s charter, which promised 20 birds annually for two decades.

Sources indicate that that same year, Martins and his team discovered the lifeless body of a Spix’s chick inside its nesting hollow. When he flagged the death to ACTP officials, the reaction was defensive. “Cromwell Purchase said, ‘You can’t tell anyone about this dead chick,’” Martins recalls. “He was fearful that ICMBio would view the project as a failure.” (Purchase says he probably meant that nobody should disclose the chick’s death before he had a chance to speak to Guth.) Soon after, Guth engineered a controversial transfer of 26 Spix’s and four Lear’s macaws from Germany to the Vantara wildlife center in India’s Gujarat State, owned by the son of India’s richest man. Conservationists had alleged for years that Vantara acquired animals on the black market, claims that Vantara denies. (Last year, an investigative committee appointed by India’s Supreme Court found no evidence of trafficking, though many conservationists dispute the verdict.) ACTP defended the transfer as a matter of avian welfare, claiming the German aviary had reached capacity after Brazil froze releases. “We were full of birds,” Crosta, ACTP’s veterinarian, told me in Tasdorf as we walked past rows of well-maintained breeding pens, accompanied by the whistles, screeches, squawks and trills of 250 rare macaws from Brazil and the Caribbean. “We can’t treat them well if we overcrowd the cages, and if there’s an outbreak of something, we’re done.”.

But the Brazilian government, which demands a say involving any transaction of Spix’s macaws, suspected the Indian transfer was a commercial deal in violation of its agreement with ACTP. Enraged, Brazil severed its partnership with ACTP. Though the German group was permitted to continue monitoring the birds at the aviary and prepare for another release, Brazil was coming to regard the outfit as a rogue operation that required tighter scrutiny. “ICMBio believed that ACTP wasn’t being transparent enough to establish a healthy partnership,” Martins remarked. “And the folks at ACTP felt that ICMBio was getting in the way.”.

In early 2025, ACTP field researchers observed a fledgling, wild-hatched Spix’s macaw with severe feather loss struggling to remain airborne. “The team shrugged it off, saying, ‘It’s fighting between the birds,’” recalls Estênio Marques de Lima, a Petrolina veterinarian who spent a year at the ACTP aviary. To Marques de Lima, however, the diagnosis was clear. “This was textbook circovirus,” he told me. “Which means it was contagious as hell.” On May 12, the center notified authorities that seven of its birds had tested positive for the pathogen, including the wild fledgling and six being prepared for release.

In a recent development, alarmed, ICMBio officials entrusted the response to Sacramento, its top infectious disease specialist. Born in rural Mato Grosso State at the edge of the Amazon, Sacramento had built a reputation as an expert on the fish of freshwater ecosystems. She knew she had to move fast: The circovirus pathogen was highly contagious, especially among young birds, spreading easily through fecal matter, mucus and feather dust. Left unchecked, she says, it had the potential to ravage dozens of other parrot species that had turned the Caatinga into a favorite destination for biologists, amateur ornithologists and adventure tourists.

In a recent development, ACTP, meanwhile, disclaimed all responsibility, saying the pathogen could have come from a wild Brazilian parrot or even a pet bird sold in a local market. “We are very close to the creek system, and there’s constant interaction between wild birds and the Spix’s macaws,” Purchase told me. In addition, he stated, free-flying native macaws often visited the outdoor breeding pens, drawn by curiosity about the captive flock, where they would hang on the fence—near enough to the captive birds to spread an infection. ACTP downplayed the danger, saying the virus had probably been circulating around Brazil for three decades without causing harm.

Skeptical, Sacramento began a line-by-line review of import documents that had accompanied the latest shipment from Guth’s German aviary: 41 Spix’s macaws flown across the Atlantic in January 2025. As she pored over clearances, Sacramento found a document showing that one Spix’s macaw had initially tested positive for circovirus in a German lab before leaving Europe. “At no point did ACTP communicate with ICMBio to say, ‘This one bird came back positive; how do we deal with it?’” Sacramento noted. Instead, “They told us, ‘All of them are good.’” When ICMBio officials confronted ACTP, Crosta insisted that the initial finding was a “weak” positive. A second test at the same lab had shown the first result to be a “technical error,” he said, and both results had been noted in the documents. “There is no doubt that the animal was negative,” Crosta told me.

Recent findings suggest that but Sacramento and other experts question that verdict, saying that there’s no such thing as a “weak” positive—and that the circovirus can become latent after a positive screening and reappear with newly introduced virulence. Moreover, they say, it is highly unlikely that a wild Brazilian bird could have transmitted the virus, which originated in Australia and has been found in wild parrot populations only in parts of Oceania, Southeast Asia and Africa. In Brazil, the virus has been seen in captive parrots and other psittacines and those known to have interacted with them. Given the reintroduction center’s extreme remoteness, however, the chances that any bird, even if exposed elsewhere, could reach the area were vanishingly small. Far more likely, many experts say, the pathogen originated in Guth’s aviary, which mixed parrot species in a high-density population ideal for spreading a virus.

Industry observers note that guth notes the idea that his Spix’s macaw was “patient zero” makes no sense. “Why should we invest so much money and risk our own birds’ survival?” he asked me. “Why should I bring the virus into my own program?” Moreover, he stated, the bird he sent to Brazil spent six months in quarantine in Petrolina with 40 other Spix’s macaws, and not a single other bird became infected. (The birds that later tested positive, Purchase explained, were part of a separate cohort that, he said, almost certainly interacted with wild macaws.) “It is impossible,” Guth said, that his bird was a carrier.

In September 2025, Sacramento demanded that ACTP round up all the released birds for immediate testing. Purchase and his team refused, arguing that trapping them would subject them to stress and lower their immune response, with possibly fatal results. ICMBio should first sweep the wilderness for feathers, feces and other avian material, they argued, and only if that tested positive would ACTP comply with the order. Some experts say ACTP was clearly willing to risk the spread of virus in the wild rather than terminate the project. “Biosecurity is everything when you’re working on cases like this,” Reillo told me. “The first thing you do is recall all the birds for comprehensive testing. You say, ‘Let’s figure out what’s going on.’”.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Sacramento and her team inspected the re-introduction facility, and she states the irregularities were deeply troubling. The staff mixed infected and uninfected birds in the same pens and neglected disinfectant protocols, and handlers walked between aviaries in casual flip-flops instead of changing into sterile booties. Purchase acknowledges mixing the birds, but he says ACTP had little choice: Even birds that tested negative may have been silently incubating the virus, so moving them to quarantine with sick birds would doom them, and moving them to other pens could have spread the virus further. Instead, he says, they decided to “wait out the storm, testing regularly and removing positive birds as they became positive,” until they found sufficiently isolated aviaries on a neighboring property “which allowed us to make better separation.” He also argues that ACTP staff, by slipping into a new set of flip flops before entering each pen, maintained sterile conditions, but to Sacramento’s eye the shortcut was a failure of containment—making it easy to trail virus-infected feather dust and feces into pens filled with uninfected birds.

On November 2, 2025, federal police arrived in Curaçá, brandishing a court order to recapture the 11 remaining released macaws. Over the next seven days, Sacramento and her team cut off their food, lured them from the forest canopy and locked them into cages. A laboratory in São Paulo tested feathers, blood and PCR cloacal swabs and found that all 11 birds had the circovirus; some suffered from disfiguring symptoms such as the splintered beak, which made eating nearly impossible. Sacramento’s team unearthed 23 additional positive cases festering within the facility’s supposedly secure captive population—evidence, she says, that ACTP’s antivirus safeguards were ineffective. Crosta insists that ACTP’s own PCR screenings in a more “reliable” Berlin lab showed a far lower number: Only 2 of the 11 released birds tested positive. He suggests the Brazilian lab mishandled the samples. “We used a lab that was working for more than ten years with circovirus,” he told me. “There was less risk of contamination.”.

In a recent development, purchase and his colleagues maintain that while a handful of birds have shown severe symptoms of the disease, the wider ecological threat is limited. White, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife officer who advised the program, supports their position. “Recapturing those wild birds and bringing them back to captivity, in the absence of any clear evidence of an existential threat to the wild...was a huge overreaction,” he states. ACTP characterizes the police raid as an act of bureaucratic overreach masquerading as conservation. “It looks like the Brazilians wanted to take back control,” Purchase told me. “It’s about Brazilian pride in wanting to own everything.” Sacramento argues that by the time the police intervened, the question was no longer who controlled the project but whether the country’s native parrots could be protected from it.

In a recent development, the federal intervention, called “Operation Blue Hope,” brought one of the 21st century’s boldest reintroduction efforts to a screeching halt. In Brazil, the remaining captive Spix’s macaws—the infected and the healthy alike—now dwell in small cages in a state of indefinite quarantine. Because circovirus had never before been seen in Spix’s macaws, ICMBio is monitoring the sick birds to understand its long-term effects while seeking a treatment or a cure. The Brazilian government insists the birds will not be euthanized, and some Brazilian veterinarians are holding out hope that the South American parrots may be spared the severest symptoms seen in their Australian counterparts, and that many might survive. (Not a single Spix’s macaw has yet died from the disease.).

This article is a selection from the December 2026 matter of Smithsonian magazine.

Industry observers note that guth’s compound in Germany, meanwhile, now houses 204 Spix’s macaws, including dozens of chicks that were once slated for a triumphant trans-Atlantic release into the wild. ICMBio fined ACTP the equivalent of about $330,000 for negligence in handling biosecurity protocols, and the Brazilian Federal Police rolled out criminal investigations, confiscating phones, laptops and other evidence to determine how the virus spread. Guth, in turn, told me he planned to file his own lawsuits in Brazil, demanding that the Brazilian government prove that the circovirus originated in his aviary in Germany, though no such legal action has yet been taken. “This was my dream, but this country is so ungrateful for what I have done,” he mentioned.

Guth’s critics say the outbreak demonstrates the dangers of placing such a sensitive project in the hands of a controversial breeder with a reputation for bending the rules. One leading American parrot researcher, who asked to remain unnamed because he regularly interacts with figures from across the parrot conservation world, draws a contrast with the World Parrot Trust, which has successfully overseen reintroductions of endangered parrots across Latin America, and with far smaller budgets. In Costa Rica, a 16-year effort has returned 130 great green macaws to the wild. At Copán, in Honduras, about 150 scarlet macaws again fly above Maya ruins rich in parrot iconography. “We’re in this situation because someone played fast and loose with the rules and set back parrot conservation in Brazil and the rest of the region,” the researcher claims. “The question is: For how long? Could it be decades? For me, that’s the scary part.”.

Sources indicate that marcelo Marcelino, ICMBio’s director, insists that Brazil hasn’t ruled out seeking another partner if circumstances allow it. “We’re testing other bird species in the Caatinga, taking samples of the environment, such as feathers, to check if traces of circovirus exist,” he said. “If it’s a safe environment, we’ll begin the project again.” Mongabay recently reported that Brazil has held preliminary discussions with Vantara, the Indian wildlife center, about a potential future partnership. For now, however, Brazilian officials say their priority is to make sure that the circovirus doesn’t become a regional calamity.

Near the end of my trip, I drove 110 miles southeast of Curaçá to the Canudos Biological Station, where I checked into a spartan lodge used mostly by scientific researchers. At 4 a.m. the next day, Guilherme Feitosa, a park ranger, picked me up in his truck, and for an hour we raced along a red-earth track, then parked and hiked across a moonscape of gullies, soft sand and fractured rock.

The Canudos preserve is home to the nesting grounds of the Lear’s macaw, another endangered blue parrot, about three times the size of the Spix’s, that nests inside cavities in eroded sandstone cliffs. Feitosa and his colleagues have been carrying out a perilous task: rappelling into the canyons to collect blood samples from chicks to test them for the circovirus.

In a recent development, fifty years ago, the Lear’s population had dwindled to just 54 birds, but ICMBio’s Lear’s Macaw Integrated Management Program—in which employees plant fruit-bearing trees, monitor nests and enlist local populations to report traffickers—has brought the numbers up dramatically in two generations. There are now some 2,500 birds. If the circovirus escapes the Spix’s reintroduction area, however, their survival will once again be in jeopardy.

Sources indicate that at first light, Feitosa and I reached the rim of a sandstone canyon nearly 400 feet deep. Its walls were honeycombed with small caves where the parrots nest beyond the reach of most predators, including black-chested buzzard-eagles. Ten days before my visit, Feitosa had strapped on a harness, descended the cliff face and shone a flashlight into each cavity until he found a chick. “We’ve counted between 200 and 220 inside this canyon,” Feitosa noted. “Some of these cavities are like mazes. The nests can be 20 meters deep inside the cave.” The chicks responded by rolling onto their backs and feigning death, an instinctive defense that made it easier to draw blood from a vein beneath the wing. Now Feitosa was waiting nervously to receive the findings from a laboratory in São Paulo. “The chicks that we’ve tested haven’t shown any signs of sickness—they looked healthy,” he said. But even a single positive test could have disastrous consequences for the species. Weeks later, to the relief of Feitosa and many others, the results came back negative.

In a recent development, as the eastern sky brightened, the first faint calls echoed from below. One macaw pair climbed out of the canyon, then another. Within minutes the silence gave way to an explosion of screeches. Blue parrots streamed from the cliffs in every direction, crossing a dawn sky streaked with ribbons of orange and pink. Some flew in pairs, others in trios, others in flocks of five or ten. The birds spread across the terrain, coming to rest on cactuses or licuri palms. From another canyon a mile away came a second chorus of cries, until it seemed that the entire landscape was erupting in pandemonium. The spectacle brought the fates of two of the world’s most endangered bird species into poignant focus. Lear’s macaws still belong to the wilderness. Spix’s macaws languish in cramped cages, their uncertain future tangled up in forced quarantines, judicial warrants and competing claims on the truth.

In Berlin, I asked Guth what he thought of Marcelino’s suggestion that Brazil might restart the Spix’s reintroduction program with another partner. He countered that rebuilding it from scratch would be a monumental undertaking. “They have to figure out how to make the birds fly again,” he told me. “I guarantee that you will not see any bird flying over the next 10 or 20 years.” In the next breath, however, he insisted that he would be prepared to help, should anyone ask. “I will make my birds available,” he told me. “Why not?”.

Joshua Hammer is a contributing writer to Smithsonian magazine and the author of several books, including The Bad-Ass Librarians of Timbuktu: And Their Race to Save the World's Most Precious Manuscripts and The Falcon Thief: A True Tale of Adventure, Treachery and the Hunt for the Perfect Bird.

Miguel Monteirois a photographer and biologist who focuses on conservation projects with a special interest in endangered species.

#294. PV and batteries could help cut global power costs by 40% in 2030s

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1028 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

PV and batteries could help cut global power costs by 40% in 2030s

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PV and battery energy storage could reduce total global electricity system costs by up to 40% in the 2030s, according to a latest study by the Schneider Electric Research Institute (SERI).
  • The report, “System Costs of Electricity: A Newly introduced Baseline for the 21st Century Economy,” evaluates 40,500 scenarios involving different combinations of solar generation, battery systems and grid infrastructure.
  • The analysis considers not only the installation and operating costs of distributed systems, but also the fixed and variable costs of centralized generation and transmission and distribution infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PV and battery energy storage could reduce total global electricity system costs by up to 40% in the 2030s, according to a latest study by the Schneider Electric Research Institute (SERI). The potential savings depend on lower installation costs for the technologies and simultaneous growth in electricity demand.

The report, “System Costs of Electricity: A Newly introduced Baseline for the 21st Century Economy,” evaluates 40,500 scenarios involving different combinations of solar generation, battery systems and grid infrastructure. It uses a total system cost model to assess whether large-scale adoption of distributed energy resources (DERs), particularly rooftop solar and batteries, could make electricity cheaper or more expensive for the economy as a whole.

The analysis considers not only the installation and operating costs of distributed systems, but also the fixed and variable costs of centralized generation and transmission and distribution infrastructure. It aims to assess the economic effects of integrating these technologies across the electricity system under different regional conditions and consumption profiles.

In a recent development, using current global average installation costs for solar and batteries, the lowest modeled total system cost is $0.145/kWh, compared with a baseline of $0.160/kWh. This represents a reduction of about 10%.

Using projected installation costs for the 2030s, the minimum modeled cost falls to $0.094/kWh, about 40% below the baseline. The potential savings could add up to 0.8% to global gross domestic product (GDP) in the 2030s, compared with approximately 0.1% under current cost conditions.

According to recent reports, the report emphasizes that results vary by market. In the United States, for example, residential solar installation costs are about three times the global average. Under those conditions, the minimum modeled total system cost rises to $0.191/kWh, approximately 20% above the $0.160/kWh baseline.

Industry observers note that one of the study’s main findings is that expanding solar generation and battery capacity in isolation does not guarantee lower electricity system costs. Electrification of additional consumption sectors needs to advance alongside the deployment of distributed energy resources.

According to recent reports, the report identifies two main mechanisms behind the potential savings. The first is the displacement of grid-supplied electricity. Every megawatt-hour generated and consumed locally by a solar system reduces the need to purchase electricity from the grid. In many of the markets analyzed, the cost of distributed energy resources is already lower than the price of electricity supplied by the centralized system.

In a recent development, the second mechanism is more efficient use of existing infrastructure. Batteries can reduce peak demand and smooth consumers’ load profiles, freeing up capacity on the grid. When new electrified loads use that available capacity, fixed infrastructure costs can be spread across a larger volume of electricity sales, lowering the cost per megawatt-hour.

Potential sources of additional demand include electric vehicles, heat pumps, air conditioning systems and data centers. Combined with the flexibility provided by batteries, these loads could improve the utilization of existing assets and reduce the need for upcoming generation and grid infrastructure investments.

The study estimates that distributed energy resources could supply more than 7,500 TWh of electricity today, equivalent to approximately 30% of global electricity demand. By 2050, that potential could reach 25,000 TWh.

The sequence of investment in solar generation, batteries and electrification also affects the economic results. The study models three energy transition pathways through 2050, based on different rates of supply and demand growth.

In the first scenario, electricity demand grows ahead of the expansion of distributed energy resources. Newly introduced consumption peaks require grid upgrades and additional generation capacity, pushing total system costs to approximately $0.173/kWh in 2035.

According to recent reports, in the second scenario, solar and battery deployment precedes demand growth. Underutilized capacity can raise costs to approximately $0.168/kWh around 2030. The economic benefits emerge later, as newly introduced electrified loads begin using the available capacity.

The third pathway assumes coordinated growth in distributed generation, batteries and electricity demand. In this scenario, total system costs reach a lower peak of approximately $0.163/kWh and remain below the other pathways throughout the modeled period, falling to about $0.105/kWh in 2050.

Sources indicate that the research also highlights the importance of appropriate battery sizing. A mismatch between the storage durations selected for different types of installations can increase total system costs by as much as 35% above the current baseline, even under global average installation cost assumptions.

The study also examines investment decisions by households, commercial buildings and industrial facilities, assuming each consumer sizes its solar and battery systems to minimize its own electricity bill.

Even when each group makes decisions independently, without knowing what other consumers will choose, the results remain close to the lowest-cost configuration for the electricity system as a whole. Using projected costs for the 2030s, individual decisions produce a result within $0.002/kWh of the modeled system-wide optimum.

Performance nevertheless depends on the configuration selected. Under current global average cost conditions, an unsuitable battery configuration can cause total system costs to range from 10% below the baseline to 35% above it.

Commercial buildings, such as offices, consistently have the lowest total costs among the categories analyzed because their periods of peak consumption coincide with periods of higher solar generation.

Based on its findings, SERI identifies three priorities for realizing the economic benefits of distributed generation and batteries.

The first is to smooth electricity demand through time-of-use tariffs, demand charges and incentives for combining solar systems with batteries. On-site energy management can also help reduce peak demand and free up grid capacity.

Sources indicate that the second is to synchronize supply expansion with demand growth. The study recommends incentives that combine investment in distributed energy resources with electrification, as well as building requirements that consider these technologies together.

Industry observers note that the third is to develop supply chains and accelerate cost reductions. Suggested measures include public procurement, manufacturing incentives, streamlined permitting and workforce training for system installation.

In a recent development, the potential cost reductions depend on coordinated operation of the technologies and the development of fresh electricity loads capable of using the available supply. Expanding solar generation and batteries alongside rising demand could also support energy security and competitiveness, according to Schneider Electric.

#292. How Did Our Galaxy End Up in the Shape of a Spiral? And More Questions From Our Readers

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (589 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

How Did Our Galaxy End Up in the Shape of a Spiral? And More Questions From Our Readers

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Milky Way has spiral-shaped arms, but its inner region is more complex, with a stellar bulge in the middle and a long bar running through its center.
  • With so many birds flying around my neighborhood, why don’t I see dead birds unless they’re killed by a cat or by hitting a window?
  • In a recent development, it’s worth noting that cats and window strikes truly are major sources of mortality for birds—together accounting for roughly three billion deaths each year in the United States alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why is the Milky Way shaped like a spiral?

It has been revealed that the Milky Way has spiral-shaped arms, but its inner region is more complex, with a stellar bulge in the middle and a long bar running through its center. The cause of these spiral arms has been elusive for decades. Recent work supports a picture in which colliding galaxies, or even small gravitational tugs from orbiting bodies, can create instabilities that lead to spirals. Galaxy collisions can also compress and disturb gas and dust in ways that create strange arcs, rings and spoke-like structures. Such shapes can be seen in the Cartwheel Galaxy, for example, where they arose from its collision with a smaller companion about 400 million years ago. Collisions like these sometimes lead to vastly enhanced star formation—a phenomenon known as a starburst. In a single year, a starburst galaxy can create enough stars to equal, or even exceed, 1,000 times the mass of our sun. For comparison, our own Milky Way galaxy creates only about two suns’ worth of fresh star mass every year. —Matthew Ashby, chair of the Center for Astrophysics’ Optical and Infrared Astronomy Division, Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.

With so many birds flying around my neighborhood, why don’t I see dead birds unless they’re killed by a cat or by hitting a window?

In a recent development, it’s worth noting that cats and window strikes truly are major sources of mortality for birds—together accounting for roughly three billion deaths each year in the United States alone. But when birds die of other causes, the evidence is harder to find. I would expect a sick or aging bird to instinctively move somewhere sheltered—but this is a guess. Until very recently, most birds were too small to be fitted with trackers. But miniature GPS tracking tags and radio telemetry transmitters now allow us to study smaller birds. We will soon have more understanding of how they behave in the lead-up to death and what might happen to their carcasses, both of which are important for conservation. —Scott Yanco, migratory bird research ecologist, Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute.

Where did the skateboarding halfpipe get its name? Did people use to skate inside actual pipes?

Recent findings suggest that the skateboarding halfpipe does get its name from actual pipes. In 1975, Tom Stewart traveled to the Arizona desert to skate the enormous concrete pipes associated with a federal public works project bringing water from the Colorado River to major cities. Inside these pipes, skateboarders could use gravity to gain the speed they needed for ambitious tricks. With the help of his architect brother, Stewart designed and built the first official skateboarding halfpipe in 1977, mimicking the shape of “half a pipe.” Stewart had his brother draw up blueprints for the design, and he began selling the template for $19.99. Soon, halfpipes were showing up in yards across the country and around the world. Over time, the shape transformed into the flat-bottomed halfpipe we know today. By 1983, this design also made its way into snowboarding, as athletes transferred skateboarding tricks onto snow. Freestyle skiing and BMX soon followed. The ESPN X Games, which introduced in 1995, helped establish the halfpipe as a catalyst for the aerial tricks of extreme sports. —Jane Rogers, curator, division of culture and the arts, National Museum of American History.

#291. How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (826 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite.
  • But these leftovers aren’t all space junk.
  • A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

But these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

In a recent development, early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, says Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”.

It has been revealed that leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

It has been revealed that other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

Images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

The moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

But some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley says samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” claims Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

What would happen if Yellowstone’s ‘supervolcano’ erupted today?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

According to recent reports, ahead of plans by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

Sources indicate that “You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” states Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) strategy to adopt this reusable design.

According to recent reports, even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley claims the ESA has made plans to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into upcoming materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley says that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” says Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”.

It has been revealed that that lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

Latest Update: These London Apartments Look Straight Out of the Stone Age. Could They Be the Future of Sustainable Architecture?

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From low-carbon concrete to mass timber to green steel, architects across the globe are employing cutting-edge technology to revolutionize eco-friendly building design.
  • With a hulking, pink exoskeleton decorated with Celtic patterns, Petra Heights, a trio of apartment towers ranging from six to 10 stories, looks straight out of the Stone Age.
  • “All of the weight of the building is coming down the stone, and all the wind load is carried by the stone,” the project’s engineer, Steve Webb, co-founder of engineering firm Webb Yates, tells Dezeen’s Jennifer Hahn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From low-carbon concrete to mass timber to green steel, architects across the globe are employing cutting-edge technology to revolutionize eco-friendly building design. But the team behind a new north London apartment complex argues the industry’s path forward may lie in the ways of the past.

With a hulking, pink exoskeleton decorated with Celtic patterns, Petra Heights, a trio of apartment towers ranging from six to 10 stories, looks straight out of the Stone Age. That’s fitting, as the development’s load-bearing structures and decorative cladding are one and the same: stacks of raw, unchiseled stone.

“All of the weight of the building is coming down the stone, and all the wind load is carried by the stone,” the project’s engineer, Steve Webb, co-founder of engineering firm Webb Yates, tells Dezeen’s Jennifer Hahn. Altogether, the complex houses a ground-floor storefront, two rooftop gardens and 22 apartments.

Petra Heights is part of an ongoing collaboration between architecture firm Groupwork, headed by Amin Taha, and Webb Yates to popularize stone as a viable alternative to steel and cement, which together represent 16 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.

The stone frame—made of pink basalt from Sicily and larvikite from Norway—produces fewer carbon emissions than traditional steel-and-concrete models. With a stone external frame and a concrete internal frame, the Petra Heights project produced around 30 percent less carbon emissions than a fully steel or concrete alternative, the Guardian’s Oliver Wainwright reports. Those savings could rise to 95 percent with domestically-mined stone, per Dezeen.

Industry observers note that the two men began looking into stone 15 years ago after running into roadblocks while collaborating on a steel frame. A conservation officer pointed them towards stone. Skeptical, they asked a stonemason about the feasibility of building with the material, the Architect's Newspaper’s Richard Martin reports.

“Are you completely stupid?” Webb recalls the mason saying, according to the Architect’s Newspaper. “Just look around London—it’s been all stone for the last one thousand years. It’s still standing. Of course you can build in stone.”.

Recent findings suggest that since then, they have continually pushed the edge of what stone and wood can do. In 2021, the pair’s six-story 15 Clerkenwell Close, featuring a load-bearing stone structure, was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize, the United Kingdom’s most prestigious architecture award. Petra Heights is their biggest concept yet.

To demonstrate the strength and flexibility of stone, Webb Yates, in collaboration with the Stonemasonry Manufacturer, designed Stone Space Frame, a nearly 15-foot-tall electricity pylon prototype which requires steel only for tension.

In a recent development, the project used 1,000 tons of rock to form nearly 600 stone columns and lintels. It also features the world’s first fully stone elevator shaft. With no steel reinforcement or secondary structure, Petra Heights is the largest load-bearing stone structure since the great stone cathedrals, the project’s website boasts. And Webb and Ahan aren’t stopping there.

Recent findings suggest that “If we build another one, it can be taller, higher, stronger,” Webb tells Dezeen. In 2020, the duo released a concept for a 30-story office block with a stone exoskeleton.

Recent findings suggest that currently, Groupwork is working on another stone-bearing mixed-use development in east London. Combined with dowel-laminated timber walls and floors, photovoltaic panels and a canal water source heat pump, the structure will generate 135 percent of its energy needs, making it “carbon negative” by selling energy back to the grid.

Webb’s next venture is a 650-foot stone skyscraper sans the usual concrete core and columns. It will feature heavy, dark granite at the base and lighter, thinner limestone towards the top, optimizing the different load-bearing features of the two stones.

“The impact of removing the concrete core from high rises has a big carbon benefit,” Webb tells Dezeen. But he claims the next big push of load-bearing stone structures may be even better focused on smaller buildings, particularly as the United Kingdom pushes to deliver on its promise to build 1.5 million newly introduced homes before 2029. “Get rid of all the brickwork, get rid of all the concrete cores from concrete medium rise housing, [that] will put a big dent in the carbon footprint of the million homes," he adds.

In a recent development, the two firms have even made a potential model, a “stone demonstrator house” that uses pre-tensioned stone beams and columns; stone floor slabs; and a self-supporting stone facade. The prototype reduces carbon emissions by 70 percent from a reinforced concrete frame and 90 percent from a steel one.

Webb states these stone designs are more than just climate friendly. They provide a wellspring of creative potential for designers and builders. “It’s a massive opportunity for architects to change it up—a reason to make a fresh style,” he tells the Guardian.

Gabby Shell is an editorial intern with Smithsonian magazine.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus.
  • Editing controls could be a little more responsive.
  • Industry observers note that why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate.

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing.

2K image quality is better than we expected.

Lightweight and easy to travel with.

Editing controls could be a little more responsive.

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

In a recent development, ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

Sources indicate that with 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

According to recent reports, the Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

Industry observers note that it comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

In a recent development, on the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

It comes with a carry case, strap, USB-C cable and solar filter.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Sources indicate that it also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.).

Recent findings suggest that the Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, initiative a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

Recent findings suggest that the Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Industry observers note that click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

Sources indicate that there's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a newly introduced target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

In a recent development, the AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. We'll add more images to this review over the coming weeks. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd have ideally aimed for longer in some cases.

Sources indicate that now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

Recent findings suggest that the Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula is another lovely target where you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced people will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Sources indicate that still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you want better image quality.

In a recent development, if you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

Read our full Seestar S30 Pro review.

If you want a longer focal length.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

Read our full Seestar S50 Pro review.

If you want a more traditional telescope.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review.

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.
