#167. Industry News: Voyager 1 is almost one light-day away from Earth

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (860 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Industry News: Voyager 1 is almost one light-day away from Earth

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that voyager 1, the NASA space probe that has traveled farther from Earth than any other human-made object, is closing in on a remarkable milestone.
  • It has been revealed that at that moment, a radio signal sent from Earth would take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and then it would take another 24 hours for the probe’s response to come back.
  • Communicating with a machine at this superlative distance is “a pretty incredible endeavor,” Princeton University research scientist and heliophysicist Jamie S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1, the NASA space probe that has traveled farther from Earth than any other human-made object, is closing in on a remarkable milestone. Actually, let’s call it a 16.09-billion-milestone. That’s the distance a photon can travel in a single day, which is to say the Voyager 1 spacecraft will be exactly one light-day away from our planet on November 18 at 5:18 a.m. EST.

It has been revealed that at that moment, a radio signal sent from Earth would take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and then it would take another 24 hours for the probe’s response to come back. Imagine on a Friday morning telling your oven to turn on, but you don’t receive confirmation that it’s hot until Sunday. And by that point, the oven would have been baking whatever was inside for most of Saturday. That is the kind of delay that NASA’s Voyager team must work with.

Communicating with a machine at this superlative distance is “a pretty incredible endeavor,” Princeton University research scientist and heliophysicist Jamie S. Rankin tells Popular Science. Rankin is also a deputy project scientist of the Voyager mission. “In my mind the fun is receiving a signal back from the Voyager, a light-day away.”.

According to recent reports, rankin and other astronomers use those signals to study the very local interstellar medium, which is the suburb of space surrounding our solar system. Voyager 1 has been in this region, about 11 billion miles away, since 2012. There, the probe can detect changes in plasma and the magnetic field.

“Right now we’re trying to figure out how far out are the influences of the sun felt,” she states.

The sun continuously spits out charged particles in a stream of solar wind that extends into space. That wind pushes back against the gas and other interstellar stuff surrounding our solar system, sculpting a bubble in space known as the heliosphere. “There will be some part farther out, some distance away [where the] interstellar medium has no idea that the heliosphere is even there,” she says. Rankin adds that she thinks Voyager 1 is right on the edge of this “undisturbed, pristine interstellar medium.”.

It is something of a marvel that the almost 50-year-old Voyager 1 continues to supply astronomers with data. To send information to Earth, the probe uses a 23-watt radio transmitter (about the output of a small refrigerator lightbulb). Only antennas as sensitive as the 70-meter-wide dishes in the NASA Deep Space Network can detect Voyager 1’s super-faint signal. Without them, the space probe would have gone incommunicado years ago.

When Voyager 1 debuted in September 1977, the nuclear-powered spacecraft had 10 operational scientific instruments. It discovered new moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn on its way out of our solar system; its observations of Jupiter’s moon Europa hinted at a liquid ocean under an icy crust. When the probe traveled beyond our solar system’s planets, NASA’s Voyager team shut down unnecessary equipment to conserve power. Now only two of its instruments are active. Ongoing management continues to preserve as much juice as possible from the spacecraft’s dwindling plutonium supply. The team was also forced to turn off the Low-energy Charged Particles experiment in April. In September, NASA swapped out three systems for lower-power alternatives on the Voyager 1, about six weeks after the same strategy worked on its twin Voyager 2 probe.

“It’s fun to see what sort of innovation people come up with to keep the spacecraft going,” Rankin says. “There’s only so much you can turn off.”.

Voyagers 1 and 2 have been operating without several instrument heaters for years. If shutting those off hadn’t worked, Rankin notes “the mission would have ended a decade ago.”.

Recent findings suggest that still, its operational margins are thin. In late October, NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1; that glitch has appeared to resolve itself and may have been related to a group of thrusters going offline.

“This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,” Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in a news release. “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.” (JPL representatives did not respond to Popular Science’s requests for comment.).

All spacecraft missions must come to an end, no matter how plucky the probe or innovative its engineering team. NASA estimates that the Deep Space Network will lose contact with Voyager 1 around 2036, long before it travels to its two-light-day milestone. The probe may also freeze, unable to point properly back at Earth. Or its power systems will finally go kaput.

Sources indicate that “We know that’s coming at some point. It’s probably not 20 years from now,” Rankin says. “It’s probably not 10 years from now.”.

And then Voyager 1 will go forever radio silent as it cruises onward through the heavens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that australia’s broad-headed snake (Hoplocephalus bungaroides) is as unique as it is threatened. However, ecologists at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) have good news about this reptile. According to researchers, four of six captive-bred juveniles recently released into the Australian bush have survived their initial, most dangerous months outdoors. The team’s first-of-its-kind program may provide a promising path forward for the species—and a set of bespoke, artificial rocks may be the key.

Sources indicate that “Reintroducing any threatened species is challenging, especially when they’re captive bred,” explained University of Technology Sydney (UTS) wildlife ecologist Jonathan Webb. “When the juvenile snakes are released, they risk getting eaten by either native predators, like kookaburras and brown snakes, or invasive predators such as cats or foxes.”.

The broad-headed snake’s current predicament is the result of multiple concerns. The distinct, yellow-banded serpent is slow to mature, and only begins reproducing around five years old. When it does, the nearly three-foot-long snake is one of the only venomous species known to give birth to live offspring. Although adults can live as long as 23 years in their native Sydney Basin, females only mate every two or three years. This leaves the broad-headed snake extremely susceptible to climate change, human impacts, and invasive predators. Any disruptions to the reproductive cycle can destabilize Australia’s population for generations—and the species has experienced plenty of disruptions over the last few decades.

“The broad-headed snake fascinated me because it used to be very common in the Sydney region, but even in the 1990’s it was quite rare,” noted Webb. “Why was this species in trouble when other snake species were doing okay?”.

Webb noted that Australia’s increasingly frequent droughts and wildfires, coupled with habitat destruction, have made the broad-headed snake one the continent’s most threatened species. The intentional removal of bush-rocks for landscaping projects is also rough on the animals.Juveniles are particularly hard hit, as they rely on the bush-rocks for shelter and a steady diet of other reptiles like skinks and geckos.

Industry observers note that “You can still buy rocks and boulders taken from the bush at your local landscape supplier, which is something I find really frustrating,” said Webb, adding that a single attractive boulder can sell for as much as $450. “That’s a pretty strong incentive for people.”.

According to recent reports, in collaboration with the conservation organization Aussie Ark and Indigenous representatives of the Traditional Owners of the Shoalhaven region, Webb’s team have bred eight broad-headed snakes in captivity since 2024. Biologists kept one pair of snakes for their genetics, then released the other six at restoration sites in May. However, the juveniles weren’t left stranded in the bush. Researchers placed them beneath custom artificial rocks designed with ideal crevice measurements to mirror natural geologic formations’ thermal properties. Webb mentioned the rocks were “critical” to the snakes’ survival odds.

“Broad-headed snakes are nocturnal so they shelter under these rocks during the day and rely on them for warmth, protection and to attract prey,” he explained.

In a recent development, biologists hope to expand the program elsewhere in Australia, and breed even more broad-headed snakes for release. Although it’s a slow process, their early successes indicate a potentially ecosystem-altering solution for the reptiles.

“We now have a unique, multi-faceted, holistic program that’s a model for threatened species conservation Australia-wide, and I couldn’t be prouder of our team and our partners,” added Aussie Ark founder Tim Faulkner.

#163. Bald eagle Shadow defends Kaydee and his nest from intruder

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (812 w)

Bald eagle Shadow defends Kaydee and his nest from intruder

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that word to the wise: don’t mess with Shadow’s nest.
  • Sources indicate that however, just after landing, Kaydee was on high alert because another eagle was eyeing the nest from above.
  • “The brief encounter last night definitely showed Shadow and Kaydee defending the nest, protecting it and each other,” writes Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the non-profit organization that runs the livestream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that word to the wise: don’t mess with Shadow’s nest. For the first time in two weeks, the internet-famous bald eagle’s (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) vocals were heard on the camera that captures a 24/7 livestream of his nest in Southern California. Shadow’s potentially fresh partner Kaydee was also heard nearby and she landed on the nest.

Sources indicate that however, just after landing, Kaydee was on high alert because another eagle was eyeing the nest from above. Shadow swiftly responded with loud vocals, and came swooping past the nest. While the intruding eagle briefly followed Shadow away, it made a turn back towards the nest. Kaydee made more calls to Shadow and quickly flew out of the nest, as the intruder tried to land on the branches above her. Shadow returned to the nest, and put himself between Kaydee and the intruder above, and all three birds flew away. Eventually, Shadow perched on a nearby tree and was heard giving a warning call in a loud voice while standing watch. The scene that appeared straight out of a movie was another exciting moment for the eagles of Major Bear Valley.

“The brief encounter last night definitely showed Shadow and Kaydee defending the nest, protecting it and each other,” writes Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the non-profit organization that runs the livestream. “What a delight to see them as they have truly been missed these past two weeks!”.

According to FOBBV, Shadow is ALSO an “experienced master builder and knows exactly when it’s time to begin tidying up the nest, moving stick furniture or placing new guardrails or a baby gate.”.

It has been revealed that we still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Bald eagle nesting officially begins in September, and lasts over six months, depending on when the the chicks fledge. Eggs are typically laid in January. Viewers can follow Shadow and Kaydee and their journey on the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

It has been revealed that kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Significant Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

Recent findings suggest that in January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

It has been revealed that A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Massive Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

Euclid space telescope unveils first major data release, including map of 900 million galaxies

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.
  • Recent findings suggest that on Thursday (Nov.
  • According to recent reports, "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

According to recent reports, "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery.".

It has been revealed that captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Sources indicate that gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here.".

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Recent findings suggest that among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid indicates a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope prepares to survey.

It has been revealed that this image indicates the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

Sources indicate that with about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#161. Losing even one hour of sleep can make you more susceptible to scams

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (527 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Losing even one hour of sleep can make you more susceptible to scams

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A poor sleep schedule doesn’t only affect your overall mood, energy levels, and long-term health.
  • “Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” said UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.
  • In a recent development, if you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A poor sleep schedule doesn’t only affect your overall mood, energy levels, and long-term health. Fresh evidence indicates that losing as little as one hour of rest may increase your chance of falling for an online scam by over 10 percent the following morning. Neurobiologists at the University of California, Irvine, laid out their findings in a study published today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), arguing that even minimal sleep disruptions can have almost immediate consequences.

“Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” said UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.

In a recent development, if you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone. Cybercrimes continue to increase exponentially in the United States. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center received over one million reports in 2025—a nearly 25 percent increase from only five years earlier.

Remaining aware of con artist tactics and staying up-to-date on personal cybersecurity strategies are some of the best ways to protect yourself. However, Schechtman and his colleagues recently wondered if something as seemingly inconsequential as a single evening of bad sleep may also put people at risk for schemes like an email phishing attack. To investigate, the team partnered with a large, unnamed organization as it ran a cybersecurity awareness campaign for more than 11,000 employees. Multiple times a year, the company’s IT department issued emails imitating phishing attempts, then tallied how many workers clicked through the fake malicious links. Schechtman’s team then analyzed results both before the switch to Daylight Saving Time (DST), as well as the Monday after employees lost an hour of sleep.

Industry observers note that on the Monday prior to DST, workers clicked on a phishing email link about 15.5 percent. of the time. Then, the Monday immediately following DST saw that rate rise to about 17.7 percent. That may not seem like much, but the difference comes out to about a 13 percent increase in phishing victims after losing approximately just one hour of sleep. According to Schechtman, there are multiple ways to contextualize these results.

“First, they give us a peek into the effects of very minor sleep loss… [from] Daylight Saving Time, which is similar in scope to the kind of sleep loss that many of us experience daily,” he stated. “Although we focused on cybersecurity, many of our day-to-day decisions are likely compromised in similar ways.”.

In a recent development, schechtman hopes both employers and cybersecurity companies take regularly sleep-depriving events like DST, holidays, and even primetime sporting events into consideration when advising the public on phishing awareness. In the meantime, he stressed that even those who regularly suffer from sleep challenges continue to prioritize their rest as much as possible.

“Better sleep likely leads to better decisions,” he added.

#160. Here’s how solar and wind developers can hold on to tax credits

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1077 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Canarymedia

Here’s how solar and wind developers can hold on to tax credits

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Canarymedia

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) in August 2022, solar and wind developers celebrated something that had historically been elusive: long-term certainty about federal tax incentives.
  • The One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law in July 2025, sharply shortened the timeline for wind and solar projects to claim the ITC and PTC and tightened the requirements to qualify.
  • According to recent reports, A recent Canary Media Forum, ​“Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline,” aimed to cut through that confusion and offer strategies for accessing federal incentives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) in August 2022, solar and wind developers celebrated something that had historically been elusive: long-term certainty about federal tax incentives. Companies accustomed to the waxing and waning of political support for the investment tax credit (ITC) and production tax credit (PTC) now had a decade of reliable access to both. One analysis after the law’s passage projected an additional 155 gigawatts of solar and wind capacity by 2030 and more than $270 billion in additional investments.

That certainty was short-lived. The One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law in July 2025, sharply shortened the timeline for wind and solar projects to claim the ITC and PTC and tightened the requirements to qualify. The OBBBA was expected to crush clean-energy growth. It didn’t. But one of its most immediate effects was to create confusion over who could still access the tax credits, for how long, and what requirements wind and solar companies must meet.

According to recent reports, A recent Canary Media Forum, ​“Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline,” aimed to cut through that confusion and offer strategies for accessing federal incentives. The event was sponsored by Intersolar & Energy Storage North America (IESNA) and brought together a tax attorney, a project developer, a procurement specialist, and a manufacturer, who shared their perspectives on lingering uncertainties about qualifying for credits, steps to take now, and what could change in the future.

Recent findings suggest that as the webinar’s title suggests, the end of 2027 is the deadline that matters most. ​“Those credits go away if your project isn’t placed into service by the end of 2027,” said Heather Cooper, a partner at the law firm McDermott Will & Schulte.

There is one exception to that 2027 cutoff. The OBBBA gave solar and wind projects one year to begin construction to retain tax credit eligibility, a countdown that ended July 4, 2026. Projects that met the July 4 deadline face a clock of their own. They generally have four calendar years after construction began to be placed in service. For projects that started this year, that means the end of 2030.

Those hard dates suggest that claiming the ITC and PTC is a black-and-white matter. It is not. Definitions for key terms such as ​“placed in service” and ​“begin construction” leave room for interpretation. For example, The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) lists five factors it considers when determining whether a project is in service, including whether it has secured the necessary permits and licenses, completed critical preoperation tests, and synchronized with the power grid.

Recent findings suggest that because the IRS evaluates those factors case by case, Cooper stated, a project doesn’t necessarily have to satisfy all five. That makes it hard to be certain when a project meets the criteria. Similarly, beginning construction doesn’t necessarily mean a project had modules installed by July 4.

Under IRS rules, one way to begin construction is to perform significant physical work, either on the project site or away from it. Another way to qualify is to pay or incur at least 5 percent of total project costs, often by purchasing modules or other equipment. And a developer that missed the July 4 deadline on paper may not be out of luck. Cooper said that reviewing what was done before that date, such as securing smaller equipment contracts, tracking internal costs, or starting early site work, may support a claim that construction had already begun.

For projects that didn’t begin construction by July 4, the end-of-2027 deadline forces hard choices. Rohit Patil, senior director of design engineering at Latest Leaf Energy, stated developers should review their entire portfolio to identify which projects have a realistic path to being placed in service by then and which are worth accelerating.

It has been revealed that “The placed-in-service deadline doesn’t necessarily turn a marginal project into a good project,” he said. ​“Projects with borderline economics are particularly vulnerable because they have little room to absorb any additional costs and delays.”.

Industry observers note that for many developers, the key factor that will determine whether a project can meet the in-service deadline is the utility interconnection timeline. Kleber Facchini, senior director of CC&I products and applications at SolarEdge Technologies, said customers that build both ground-mounted and rooftop systems are shifting toward rooftop projects. Those connect to the distribution grid near cities and tend to interconnect faster than ground-mounted projects, which are often sited in rural areas with weaker grids.

Equipment decisions also shape whether a project keeps its credits in two ways. The first is timing: A project can’t be placed in service by the end of 2027 without all its equipment on site.

Sources indicate that that means ordering equipment now. Facchini mentioned transformers have especially long lead times and urged developers to procure modules, racking, and trackers as well. Another reason to secure modules swiftly: Fresh Section 232 tariffs on imported polysilicon and solar products, including modules, take effect on December 4. ​“Any sort of modules that land after that date will cost you more,” said Ravi Manghani, senior director of strategic sourcing at Anza Renewables.

The second is compliance with the OBBBA’s foreign entity of concern (FEOC) rules, which can disqualify a project even if it is on schedule. The rules include denying credits to projects with too much ownership, debt, or control tied to China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran. For projects that began construction in 2026 or later, FEOC rules also cap the share of equipment that can come from manufacturers tied to those countries.

In a recent development, the underlying assumption behind the IRA was that the law would endure because many of its benefits were directed toward Republican constituencies. That turned out not to be true for wind and solar, and the OBBBA cut short the long-term support the IRA promised.

Industry observers note that one lesson from both the rollback of the IRA and past tax credit challenges is that federal energy tax policy is rarely a static and settled matter. ​“Folks who’ve been in the industry long enough know that an ITC cliff is not necessarily an ITC cliff,” Manghani said. Though not exactly a strategy for securing tax credits, it is a reminder that this year’s midterms and the 2028 presidential election could fundamentally reshape the federal incentive landscape yet again.

#159. Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (721 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it.
  • Humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing.
  • To probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it. Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) likely watch adults making different vocalization to learn how and when to use those sounds themselves, particularly when they purse their lips to blow “raspberries.” The findings detailed in a study published today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) show that the primates’ sounds are not instinctual and set in stone, as previously believed.

Humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing. For example, English speakers mimic dogs with “woof,” while French speakers say “ouaf.” When it comes to our primate relatives, biologists generally used to believe that they didn’t learn sounds from one another, and that instead biology dictated their sounds. However, that’s changing with some fresh research into two groups of Chimpanzees in a couple of west African countries.

To probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry. Chimpanzees make this unvoiced sound that’s similar to how humans push their lips together to blow raspberries. The team looked at how 91 chimpanzees, from birth to 55 years old, used the raspberry call. They studied a group of wild chimpanzees from four communities in Taï National Park, Ivory Coast, and a group of young, orphaned, and peer-raised chimpanzees at Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Sierra Leone.

The team found that the wild Ivory Coast chimpanzees almost exclusively used the raspberry while grooming others. However, the juveniles at the Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary used it across a much wider range of social situations.

If blowing a raspberry is only an instinctive call, the groups should be using it in similar ways no matter where they were raised. According to the team, these differences suggest that chimpanzees learn from adults how to make a call, as well as when and why to use it.

“In everyday communication, we use the words that we do only because our peers do too. It’s communal practice that fixes their meaning, rather than features of the words themselves,” Richard Moore, a study co-author and mind, language, and psychology philosopher at the University of Warwick, remarked in a statement.

“The discovery that this is true not just for natural languages but also some chimpanzee calls means there’s more continuity between chimpanzees’ vocal learning and our own than we previously suspected.”.

The team also say that when an adult chimpanzee was introduced to one of the groups living in the Tacugama sanctuary, the young chimps gradually began to use the raspberry more consistently and began to resemble the adult’s noises. This suggests that adults serve as role models, helping a community settle in on shared communication patterns.

It has been revealed that the researchers say this is the first time that this kind of learned and agreed-upon sound use has been shown in chimpanzee calls. The link between the raspberry sound and its use appears to be shared from one chimpanzee to another, and is not built in at birth. While chimpanzees struggle to learn entirely fresh call sounds, the study suggests that they can learn the meaning behind sounds that they already know how to make but didn’t use in the same way as other chimps.

“Even aspects of chimpanzee vocal communication that seemed fixed and unlearned may be shaped by learning, suggesting that there is still much to discover about their vocal repertoire,”.

added Antoine Valet, a study co-author and cognitive scientist at the Institute of Cognitive Sciences (CNRS) in France.

Additionally, the team has some theories on why different chimpanzee populations use the raspberry in similar ways if it is a learned sound.

Industry observers note that “One possibility is that, whilst grooming, as chimpanzees use their lips to extract parasites from another’s fur, it may be easier to generate a vocalisation that uses similar lip movements, a call that is known to prolong grooming bouts,” explained study co-author and CNRS behavioral ecologist Catherine Crockford. “Communities may have found this useful independently, but that wouldn’t change the fact that the call is a convention. We need more research to test it.”.

Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes. Prehistoric cultures unfortunately didn’t have this luxury, and often responded dramatically to such changes. In northern Peru, archaeological evidence indicates local societies sometimes even turned to mass human sacrifices in an attempt to stop destructive flooding from events like El Niño.

Recent findings suggest that that remarked, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate concerns. According to their study recently published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, such brutal moments were actually pretty rare occurrences in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley.

“The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” remarked Upcoming York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.

It has been revealed that the Lambayeque Valley is located inside northern Peru’s coastal desert, but the region has hosted residents for  6,000 years. Although the valley generally receives little rainfall, its rivers and proximity to the sea allowed communities to flourish there for generations, including societies like the Moche from roughly 100–750 CE, and the Sicán from about 750–1375 CE.

“Archaeological evidence shows that in so many ways they were mirrors of us—in how they lived their daily lives, interacted with their world, ran their economies, and confronted (and sometimes contributed to) environmental crises,” explained George Mason University archaeologist and study co-author Haagen Klaus.

Previous excavations have indicated that mass human sacrifices possibly preceded the collapse of the Moche and Sicán’s political systems. Researchers have since hypothesized that these acts likely coincided with periods of mass flooding,probably due to El Niño weather oscillations. Just like today, these weather events destroyed food stocks and disrupted agricultural production. Since large human sacrificial rituals may have been attempts by the ruling class to restore balance to nature, the team to wonder if violence was simply a more common facet of everyday life for the Moche and Sicán.

“If these big ritual sacrifices were indicative of some underlying crisis, we hypothesized that these events might have been extending into people’s everyday experience of the world,” said Snyder.

Klaus, Snyder, and their collaborators turned to the Lambayeque Valley Biohistory Project’s skeletal archive for answers. The collection spans about 3,000 years of history across 30 different archaeological sites. The team established relatively precise death estimates for over 1,600 individuals, while also examining them for evidence of intentional cranial trauma associated with human sacrifice. Contrary to their theory, only 25 remains (1.6 percent of the sample pool) showed signs of violence, while just 77 displayed indicators of accidental trauma. Of those, none were directly linked to known periods of past ecological crises.

“In Lambayeque, there’s 6,000 years of creative adaptations to El Niño and longer-term changes in climate, and widespread violence wasn’t one of them,” concluded Klaus.

According to recent reports, the study’s authors noted that because they were notable to radiocarbon date all of the remains, their findings remain broader estimates of wide time periods. At the same time, they stressed the evidence underscores humanity’s history of facing intense climate challenges not with violence, but adaptation.

According to recent reports, “This really highlights that widespread violence isn’t a predetermined response to climate change,” mentioned Snyder. “As a society, we both get to and have to choose how we respond to our own climate crisis.”.

“Violence and social unraveling are not destined outcomes, ever,” added Klaus.
